calculus.title: Read a function as a rule, a table and a graph
calculus.goal: Connect an input, its output, and a point on a graph before calculating a rate.
opening: A cyclist’s position is described by s(t)=t². Read this as an instruction: choose a time t, square it, and call the result s. In this model, t is measured in seconds and s in metres. The notation is compact, but the job is just input followed by output.
At t=2, square 2 and get 4. At t=3, get 9. The point (3,9) on the graph says that three seconds corresponds to a position of nine metres. It does not say that the speed is nine metres per second.
calculus.heading: Keep the axes attached to their quantities
teaching: Make a small table before drawing anything: t=0,1,2,3 gives s=0,1,4,9. Put time on the horizontal axis and position on the vertical. The points rise more steeply as time increases. That visual change will matter when we study velocity, but the height of the graph is still position. A graph can show a high position with a small slope, or a low position with a large slope.

Now add ten metres to the rule: s(t)=t²+10. Every position reading rises by ten, so the whole graph shifts upward. The changes between readings stay the same: from 2 to 3 seconds, position goes from 14 to 19, a change of five. Moving the origin has not made the cyclist move faster. This is a useful way to catch a later calculation that divides an absolute position by a clock reading instead of comparing changes.
terms: A rule assigning an output to each allowed input.
Position s as a function of time t in this example.

first.title: Build three points yourself
first.problem: Use s(t)=t² to find the positions at 1, 2 and 3 seconds.
steps: Replace t by 1 everywhere it appears in this rule.
The input is two seconds; the output is four metres.
Read the pair as time first, position second.
first.notice: A point on this graph records a position at a time. A rate needs a comparison between nearby points.

second.title: Shift the origin without changing the ride
second.problem: For s(t)=t²+10, compare the positions at 2 and 3 seconds.
steps: The extra ten is added to both readings.
This is the same change as 9−4 for the original rule.
The graph is ten metres higher, but the displacement over this interval is unchanged.
Position height and rate of change are different information.
second.notice: An upward shift is not an increase in velocity.

exercise: For s(t)=2t², find the position at t=3. Is your answer a position or a speed?
s(3)=2×3²=18 metres. It is a position. To calculate a velocity, compare changes in position and time or differentiate the position rule.

calculus.title: Differentiate a few terms without losing their meaning
calculus.goal: Use the constant, sum and power rules, then interpret the resulting rate.
opening: Once the idea of a derivative is clear, recalculating the limit for every polynomial is slow. The power rule packages that work: the derivative of tⁿ is ntⁿ⁻¹. For t² it gives 2t, agreeing with the shrinking-interval calculation.
The exponent comes down as a multiplier and then decreases by one. This is a rule to use after you know what rate you are finding, not a reason to forget the original quantity.
calculus.heading: Do one term at a time
teaching: Take s(t)=3t²+2t+5. The 3 multiplies every position change from t², so it also multiplies that term’s derivative: 3×2t=6t. The term 2t grows by two units for every extra unit of t, giving derivative 2. The final 5 never changes when t changes, so its derivative is zero. Add those rates: s′(t)=6t+2.

At t=2, the position is 3×4+4+5=21, while the rate is 6×2+2=14. Keeping the two calculations side by side prevents a common substitution mistake: putting t=2 into the original rule when the question asks for its derivative there. A negative coefficient also keeps its sign. If s(t)=10−t², then s′(t)=−2t; position is decreasing for positive t even when the position reading itself is still positive.
terms: The derivative of s with respect to t.
A term that does not change with the input.

first.title: Differentiate a position rule
first.problem: For s(t)=3t²+2t+5 metres, find velocity at t=2 seconds.
steps: Use the power rule on the quadratic term and the slope of a straight line on 2t.
Keep the variable until the rule is ready
This gives the rate at any time within the model.
Substitute into the derivative, not the original position expression.
first.notice: The constant changes position readings but contributes no velocity.

second.title: A positive position with a negative rate
second.problem: For s(t)=10−t², find position and velocity at t=2.
steps: The object is at the positive six-metre mark.
The minus sign stays with the changing term.
The position is decreasing at this moment. A positive location does not force a positive velocity.
second.notice: Always ask whether the number describes where something is or how its position changes.

exercise: For s(t)=2t³−4t+7, find s′(t) and its value at t=1.
The derivatives are 6t², −4 and 0, giving s′(t)=6t²−4. At t=1 the rate is 2. The units depend on the stated units of s and t.

calculus.title: Turn an antiderivative into a total change
calculus.goal: Use an antiderivative and bounds to calculate signed accumulation.
opening: Suppose velocity is v(t)=2t metres per second. We want the displacement from t=1 to t=3. The velocity changes throughout the interval, so multiplying one endpoint speed by the duration will not do.

An antiderivative reverses differentiation. Since the derivative of t² is 2t, t² is an antiderivative of our velocity. The total displacement is its ending value minus its starting value: 3²−1²=8 metres.
calculus.heading: The bounds identify which part to count
teaching: The definite integral ∫₁³2t dt names the signed area under the velocity graph between 1 and 3. The fundamental theorem connects that accumulation to an antiderivative: F(3)−F(1). Here F(t)=t² works. So does t²+100, because the extra 100 cancels when the two endpoint values are subtracted. This explains why the arbitrary constant in an antiderivative does not affect the definite integral.

Check the geometry. Velocity is 2 m/s at t=1 and 6 m/s at t=3. The region is a trapezoid two seconds wide, with average height four metres per second. Its area is 2×4=8 metres. If velocity becomes negative, the integral subtracts the area below the axis. For total distance you must split at the sign changes and add the magnitudes of the separate pieces.
terms: A function whose derivative is the given function.
The starting and ending input values in a definite integral.
A total in which negative contributions subtract.

first.title: Count displacement between two times
first.problem: Calculate ∫₁³2t dt and interpret it for v(t)=2t m/s.
steps: Do not silently replace the lower bound by zero.
The result is displacement over the stated interval.
first.notice: The subtraction removes accumulation before the starting bound.

second.title: Zero displacement can include travel
second.problem: Velocity is v(t)=2t−2 from t=0 to t=2. Find displacement and total distance.
steps: Velocity is negative before 1 and positive after it.
From 0 to 1: −1 m displacement. From 1 to 2: +1 m. Total distance = 2 m.
Take the magnitude of each segment rather than the magnitude of their already-cancelled sum.
second.notice: A definite integral of velocity gives displacement. It is not automatically total distance.

exercise: For v(t)=3t², find displacement from t=0 to t=2.
An antiderivative is t³. Evaluate 2³−0³=8 metres. Velocity is nonnegative on this interval, so total distance is also 8 metres.

physics.title: Draw the forces before choosing an equation
physics.goal: Choose one object, identify the forces on it, and add them by direction.
opening: Put a book on a table and leave it still. Gravity pulls the book down. The table pushes it up. Those are two forces on the book, even though you cannot see the contact force as a separate object.
Start the diagram by drawing only the book, then add arrows for interactions with its surroundings. Do not add an arrow called motion: motion is not another force.
physics.heading: Keep one object inside the diagram
teaching: For a 2 kg book, using g=10 m/s², the downward weight is 20 N. Because the book has no vertical acceleration, the total vertical force is zero. The table’s upward normal force is therefore 20 N in this case. Normal means perpendicular to the contact surface. It is not a rule that normal force always equals weight: an extra downward push would require a larger table force to keep the book still.

Now push the book horizontally while it slides. Add the hand’s push and friction as horizontal arrows. Keep the vertical pair in the diagram, but do not put their 20 N magnitudes into the horizontal net-force calculation. Components in different directions answer different equations. Also keep Newton’s third-law pairs straight: the book’s force on the table is not another force on the book; it belongs on the table’s diagram.
terms: The gravitational force on an object; mg near Earth’s surface in this model.
A contact force perpendicular to a surface.
A diagram of the forces acting on one chosen object.

first.title: A book resting on a horizontal table
first.problem: A 2 kg book has zero vertical acceleration. Use g=10 m/s². Find the upward table force.
steps: This arrow describes Earth’s gravitational force on the book.
Take up as positive. Zero acceleration requires zero net vertical force.
The result follows from the stated balance; it is not an automatic identity for all situations.
first.notice: An object at rest can have several nonzero forces whose vector sum is zero.

second.title: Add a hand pushing down
second.problem: The same book remains still while a hand pushes down with 6 N. Find the new table force.
steps: Add the new force on the book
20 N weight plus 6 N hand force, both downward.
The hand is a separate interaction.
Normal force is now larger than weight.
second.notice: The diagram changed, so the force equation changed too.

exercise: A sliding object has an 11 N horizontal push right and 3 N friction left. Its vertical forces balance. What horizontal force belongs in Fnet=ma?
The horizontal net force is 11−3=8 N right. The balanced vertical forces do not get added as extra horizontal force. Mass would still be needed to find acceleration.

physics.title: Follow a wave without carrying the whole medium along
physics.goal: Relate wavelength, frequency and wave speed, while separating wave travel from local motion.
opening: Shake one end of a rope up and down. A disturbance travels along the rope, but a small marked piece of rope mostly moves up and down near its own location. The traveling pattern and the local material motion are different things.

For a repeating wave, wavelength is the spacing between corresponding points such as neighboring crests. Frequency counts how many cycles pass a point each second. Multiply the spacing by the number passing per second to find the pattern’s speed.
physics.heading: Make the units explain the multiplication
teaching: If crests are 2 metres apart and three pass each second, the pattern advances three crest-spacings in one second: 3×2=6 metres. This is v=fλ. The frequency f has units 1/s, and wavelength λ has units m, leaving m/s. The formula does not say that every marked point on a rope is moving horizontally at that speed.

In a fixed medium under unchanged conditions, wave speed is often approximately fixed. Increasing the source frequency then shortens the wavelength. For sound traveling at 340 m/s, a 170 Hz tone has wavelength 2 m; a 340 Hz tone has wavelength 1 m. Frequency is associated with pitch, while amplitude is associated with the size of the disturbance. Making a tone louder does not by itself double its frequency.
terms: The spacing between corresponding points in a repeating wave.
The size of the disturbance from equilibrium.

first.title: Three crest-spacings per second
first.problem: A wave has wavelength 2 m and frequency 3 Hz. Find its speed.
steps: Each cycle corresponds to one wavelength of pattern travel.
Cycles per second times metres per cycle leaves metres per second.
The pattern travels 6 m each second.
This is not a claim that every piece of the medium travels with it.
first.notice: State whether the speed belongs to the wave pattern or the motion of a material point.

second.title: Higher pitch in the same air
second.problem: Sound speed is 340 m/s. Compare wavelengths at 170 Hz and 340 Hz.
steps: Speed is fixed in this comparison.
Doubling frequency halves wavelength when speed stays the same.
The calculation says nothing about which sound is louder.
second.notice: Say what remains fixed before predicting how two wave quantities change.

exercise: A wave speed stays 12 m/s while frequency changes from 2 Hz to 4 Hz. Find both wavelengths.
Use λ=v/f. The wavelengths are 6 m and 3 m. The frequency doubles and the wavelength halves because the speed was held fixed.

physics.title: Spread a force over an area
physics.goal: Calculate pressure and distinguish applied force from force per unit area.
opening: A force of 100 N can be spread over a broad surface or concentrated on a small one. The total force may stay the same, but the pressure changes because pressure is force divided by area.
Use P=F/A. A square metre is a large area, so one pascal—one newton per square metre—is a small pressure unit. Keep area in square metres when calculating pascals.
physics.heading: Check the area before dividing
teaching: Suppose a 100 N load rests on 0.02 m². Dividing gives 5,000 N/m², or 5,000 Pa. If the area shrinks to 0.01 m², the pressure doubles to 10,000 Pa. Nothing about the load’s total force doubled. Confusing force and pressure makes it hard to explain why narrow supports can press into a surface more strongly than broad ones.

A fluid at rest adds pressure with depth because deeper layers support more fluid above them. In a simple constant-density model, the pressure increase is ρgh. For water with density 1,000 kg/m³, g=10 m/s² and depth 2 m, the increase is 20,000 Pa. That is the increase below the surface pressure, not automatically the absolute pressure. If the surface is exposed to air, the atmospheric contribution must be added for an absolute value.
terms: Pressure relative to a chosen reference, such as the water surface.

first.title: The same load on half the area
first.problem: A 100 N force acts on 0.02 m², then on 0.01 m². Find the two pressures.
steps: Divide by the area, not its square root.
Pressure doubled; total force did not.
A force-per-area measure can change when only the area changes.
first.notice: Always include whether the answer is a force or a pressure.

second.title: Pressure two metres below a water surface
second.problem: Use ρ=1,000 kg/m³ and g=10 m/s². Find the pressure increase at 2 m depth.
steps: This assumes a static fluid with approximately constant density.
The result is the increase relative to the surface.
Absolute pressure would also include surface pressure.
Do not silently call a pressure increase the whole absolute pressure.
second.notice: A reference level matters for pressure, just as an origin matters for position.

exercise: A 60 N force is spread over 0.03 m². What pressure does it produce?
P=60/0.03=2,000 Pa. This gives force per square metre; it does not mean the force became 2,000 newtons.
